title: Traverse a linked list (start from head, follow next pointers until null, print each node's data).
keyPoints: Traversal starts at the head and follows each node's next reference until null is reached
Always use a separate current pointer for traversal and never move the head itself
Traversal is O(n) time because every node is visited once, and O(1) space because only one pointer is used
Traversal is the foundation for searching, counting, summing, and printing linked list contents
For a doubly linked list you can also traverse backward from the tail using prev references
A while loop with the condition current != null is the canonical traversal pattern

s1_definition.oneliner: Start at the head, process each node, follow next, and stop when you reach null.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Traversal** – visiting every node in a linked list exactly once by following `next` references from head to the end.
- **Current pointer** – a local variable set to `head` that moves through the list; the head reference itself must never be modified during traversal.
- **Termination** – the loop ends when `current` becomes `null`, meaning the last node has been passed.
- **Time** – O(n) because each node is visited once.
- **Space** – O(1) because only a single pointer variable is used regardless of list length.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India keeps Rajesh's pending transaction slips as a chain, each slip pointing to the next. To total up all pending amounts, a clerk starts at the first slip, reads it, follows its arrow to the next slip, reads that one, and keeps going until a slip's arrow points to nothing. At that point every slip has been read exactly once.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Traversal Step-by-Step

  head
   │
   ▼
  [TXN-001] ──> [TXN-002] ──> [TXN-003] ──> null
   current(1)    current(2)    current(3)    current = null
                                              (loop ends)
```

```text
  Traversal with Sum Accumulation

  Step 1: current = TXN-001, sum = 0 + 5000 = 5000
  Step 2: current = TXN-002, sum = 5000 + 12000 = 17000
  Step 3: current = TXN-003, sum = 17000 + 8500 = 25500
  Step 4: current = null, loop ends, return 25500
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Traversing a linked list means visiting every node exactly once by starting at the head and following each node's `next` reference until you reach `null`. You use a local pointer called `current`, set it to the head, and loop while it is not null. Inside the loop you do whatever work you need with the current node's data, and at the end of each iteration you advance `current` to `current.next`. When `current` becomes `null` you have passed the last node and the loop ends.

The most important rule is to never move the `head` pointer during traversal. The head must keep pointing at the first node so the list remains usable after the traversal completes. If you accidentally reassign `head` to `head.next` repeatedly, you permanently lose the start of the list. Always traverse with a separate `current` pointer and leave `head` untouched.

Traversal is O(n) time because every node is visited once, and O(1) space because only a single pointer variable is used. It is the foundation of nearly every linked list operation: counting, summing, searching, reversing, cycle detection, and merging all rely on the basic traversal pattern. A doubly linked list allows backward traversal from the tail using `prev` references.

In our banking system at National Bank of India, we use traversal to total up Rajesh's pending transaction amounts. A clerk walks the chain from the first transaction to the last, adding each amount to a running `BigDecimal` sum, and returns the total. The chain is needed again later for actual processing, so the clerk must use a separate pointer and leave the head intact.

Remember one sentence: traverse with a separate `current` pointer from head to null, never moving the head itself.
